Brand vs Performance Marketing: Different Time Horizons

Guidelowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 29 April 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

Brand and performance marketing are not rivals; they work on different clocks. Performance buys measurable outcomes now. Brand makes future outcomes more likely and cheaper. The best-known evidence, Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases, puts the long-run optimum near 60% brand and 40% activation for consumer brands, and 46:54 in B2B. Most small companies cannot start there. They should fund performance first, then shift a growing share toward brand as revenue allows, measuring each on its own timescale.

Marketing teams have argued about brand versus performance for as long as both words have existed. The argument is real, but it is mostly about time.

The two, defined

Performance marketing is spending aimed at a measurable outcome in a short window: a click, a lead, an account, a purchase, attributed to the spend that produced it. It is judged in days or weeks, on cost per outcome. Its tools are the auction platforms, affiliate, creator programmes on cost-per-outcome terms, programmatic optimised to conversions. Our piece on performance marketing as a way of paying sets out when those terms hold.

Brand marketing is spending aimed at changing what people know, believe or feel about the company, so that future outcomes become more likely and cheaper. It is judged over months or years, on recall, consideration, preference and, eventually, on the falling cost of performance marketing. Its tools are content, earned media, events, sponsorship, design, consistent presence and advertising that explains rather than asks.

PerformanceBrand
AimAn outcome nowMore likely and cheaper outcomes later
AudiencePeople in the marketFuture buyers, most of whom are not in the market
ClockDays to weeksMonths to years
Primary measureCost per outcome against customer valueBranded search, share of search, recall, the trend in cost per outcome
Typical toolsSearch, paid social, affiliate, creator CPA dealsContent, earned media, events, sponsorship, explanatory advertising
Failure modeRising cost per outcome as easy customers run outSpend nobody can connect to revenue

Why they look like rivals

They compete for the same budget and report on different clocks. In any given quarter, performance marketing can show what it produced and brand marketing cannot. The finance team, reasonably, funds what it can see.

Binet and Field's work on the IPA Databank, the UK's archive of effectiveness award entries, shows why the clocks differ. In their analysis, rational, activation-style messaging produced a large direct sales effect that "decays quickly"; emotional brand priming produced a smaller effect that decayed slowly and built over time. The share of emotional campaigns reporting very large profit effects rose from 13% at one year to 30% at two years and 43% at three or more. For rational campaigns the figures were 10%, 20% and 23%. A quarterly report will always favour activation.

Over several quarters, the reverse problem appears. Performance marketing on its own gets more expensive: the easiest customers are found first, the auctions get more crowded, and the company is buying every customer from scratch because nobody has heard of it. The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work that was not done.

The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work that was not done.

How they interact

Brand lowers the cost of performance. People who recognise a company click more, convert more and cost less to acquire. Binet and Field's B2B summary makes the same point: brand memories make later activation more effective, which is why brand results need a longer measurement window. Their consumer analysis also found brands with more very large brand effects saw larger reductions in price sensitivity.

The mechanism is reach into future demand. The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's John Dawes estimates that only about 5% of business buyers are in the market for a typical category in a given quarter, derived from companies changing key suppliers roughly once every five years. Performance marketing competes for the 5%. Brand work reaches the 95% who will be in the market later, so the company is familiar when they arrive.

Performance funds brand. Without a working acquisition engine, there is no revenue to invest in the slow work.

And performance generates the evidence brand needs. The language customers respond to, the objections that stop them, the segments that convert: these come from the performance side and should inform what the brand side says.

The honest constraints for a small company

A company with limited cash cannot fund work with an eighteen-month payback, however sound. The sequence for most small companies is performance first, to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost, then a growing share of budget toward owned and earned brand work as revenue allows.

Two exceptions. A company with an existing distribution asset (a founder with a following, a list, a community) can do brand work cheaply from day one, because the audience already exists. And a company in a category the ad platforms restrict is pushed toward earned and owned channels early, because the performance auctions are partly closed to it. In both cases, the usual sequence compresses.

A working division

The IPA benchmarks are long-run optima for established brands: about 60:40 brand to activation in Binet and Field's consumer work, and 46:54 in their B2B study. They are where a company should be heading, not where a company with six months of cash should start.

For a company past its first channel, a workable starting point is roughly three quarters of spend on performance, measured on cost per outcome against customer value, and roughly a quarter on brand. Then move the split toward the benchmarks as cash and payback allow.

Measure the brand quarter on its own clock. Branded search and direct traffic are free and weekly. Share of search, a brand's share of organic searches in its category from Google Trends, was shown by Les Binet in an IPA presentation to correlate with and lead market share in three consumer categories, by up to a year in cars. Recall can be surveyed where budgets allow. Above all, watch the trend in performance cost per outcome over time. Our piece on measuring brand in B2B covers share of search, shortlist rate and category entry points in detail, and demand generation economics covers the capture and creation split.

Illustrative example: moving the split
Decision
Move from 90:10 performance to brand toward 70:30 over three quarters.
Reason and owner
Cost per acquisition on the main paid channel had risen for four consecutive quarters while volume stayed flat, and branded search was flat. Owned by the head of growth, with the finance lead agreeing a payback limit for the performance share.
What changed
Branded search and direct sign-ups rose over the following two quarters, and the rise in cost per acquisition slowed. The split was held at 75:25 while the trend was confirmed.

Illustrative: a composite of a B2B software company with around 60 staff, built from patterns across engagements.

The point is not the ratio. It is that both sides are funded, both are measured on their own clock, and the company understands that the second one is what makes the first one affordable.

lowob takeaways

  • Different clocks, not different teams. Performance is judged in weeks on cost per outcome; brand over months or years.
  • Brand lowers the cost of performance. The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work not done.
  • Start where cash allows, head for the benchmark. Roughly 75:25 for a small company past its first channel, moving toward 46:54 in B2B or 60:40 in consumer markets.
  • Measure brand on its own clock. Branded search, share of search, recall and the trend in cost per outcome.

Common questions

What is the difference between brand marketing and performance marketing?

Performance marketing aims at a measurable outcome in a short window, judged on cost per outcome. Brand marketing aims at changing what people know, believe or feel about a company, judged over months or years on recall, consideration and the falling cost of performance.

What is the 60:40 rule in marketing?

Binet and Field's finding, from IPA effectiveness cases, that consumer brands grow best with about 60% of spend on brand building and 40% on activation. Their B2B study put the balance at 46:54.

How should a small company split its budget between brand and performance?

Start with performance to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost. Once past the first channel, roughly three quarters performance and a quarter brand is a workable start, moved toward the benchmarks as cash allows.

How do you measure brand marketing?

On branded search, direct traffic, share of search, recall where it can be surveyed, and above all the trend in performance cost per outcome over time.

Sources and notes

  • IPA, The Long and the Short of It, presentation by Les Binet and Peter Field. Analysis of IPA Databank effectiveness award entries, largely UK consumer brands; award entries skew to successful campaigns.
  • LinkedIn, How B2B marketing really drives growth, 16 October 2019. Platform summary of Binet and Field's B2B Institute study; LinkedIn sells B2B advertising.
  • Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Advertising effectiveness and the 95-5 rule, John Dawes, May 2021. Produced for LinkedIn's B2B Institute; the 5% is a heuristic estimate from replacement cycles.
  • IPA, Binet presents fast, cheap, predictive Share of Search metric, 14 October 2020. Three consumer categories; B2B use is by extension.
  • The comparison table, the 75:25 starting point and the example are lowob's guidance and illustration, not findings from these sources.

Next move

Chart your cost per outcome on the main paid channel by quarter for the last two years next to branded search volume. If cost is rising while branded search is flat, move a fixed slice of next quarter's budget to brand and agree in advance how you will judge it.
